rows.stem: A particle of mass m and charge q starts from rest and moves in an electric field \(\vec{E} = E_0 \hat{i}\). After travelling a distance x in the field along x-axis, the kinetic energy of the particle will be :
rows.solution:
The field is uniform and the particle starts from rest, so the work-energy theorem does the whole job: the kinetic energy gained equals the work done by the electric force.
The force on the charge is \(F = qE_{0}\), constant in both magnitude and direction, and it acts along the displacement. So over a distance x,
\(W = F x = qE_{0}x\)
Since the particle started at rest, all of this appears as kinetic energy:
\(K = qE_{0}x\)
The kinetic energy is \(qE_{0}x\). It grows LINEARLY with the distance travelled, not as \(x^{2}\), which is what the kinematic route confirms: \(v^{2} = 2ax\) with \(a = \dfrac{qE_{0}}{m}\) gives \(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = qE_{0}x\), and the mass cancels.

rows.stem: A square loop of side 50 cm is placed in a uniform magnetic field of \(3{\cdot}0\) T acting perpendicular to the plane of the loop. If the loop is rotated through an angle of \(90^\circ\) in \(0{\cdot}3\) s, the value of emf induced in the loop would be :
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: "No option is correct (Award full credit for attempting)". This is CBSE's own ruling on the question, not a disagreement with it — the value the physics gives appears among none of the four printed choices, and every candidate who attempted the question was given the mark.]
The flux through the loop is \(\phi = BA\cos\theta\). Initially the field is perpendicular to the plane of the loop, so the flux is a maximum, \(\phi_{1} = BA\); after a rotation of \(90^{\circ}\) the field lies in the plane of the loop and the flux is \(\phi_{2} = 0\).
The area is \(A = (0{\cdot}50)^{2} = 0{\cdot}25\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\), so
\(|\varepsilon| = \dfrac{\Delta\phi}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{BA}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{3{\cdot}0 \times 0{\cdot}25}{0{\cdot}3} = 2{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{V}\)
The average emf induced in the loop is \(2{\cdot}5\) V, which is not among the printed options.

rows.stem:
A plane electromagnetic wave travels through a medium and the magnetic field associated with it is given by
\(B = 5 \times 10^{-8} \sin (3 \times 10^{10} t - 150 x)\) T
where x is in metres and t is in seconds.
The velocity of the wave is :
rows.solution:
Read the wave number and the angular frequency straight off the argument of the sine. Comparing
\(B = B_{0}\sin(\omega t - kx)\) with \(B = 5 \times 10^{-8}\sin(3 \times 10^{10}t - 150x)\)
gives \(\omega = 3 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\) and \(k = 150\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\).
The wave speed is the ratio of the two:
\(v = \dfrac{\omega}{k} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{10}}{150} = 2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
The velocity of the wave is \(2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It is LESS than the speed of light in vacuum, as it must be in a medium; the refractive index here is \(\dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{2 \times 10^{8}} = 1{\cdot}5\). The amplitude plays no part in fixing the speed.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: A thin plano-convex lens and a thin equi-concave lens are kept coaxially in contact as shown in the figure. Assuming both the lenses are made of glass of refractive index \(\mu\), and R is the radius of curvature of each curved surface, the focal length of the combination is :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - a sectional drawing of the two lenses in contact, each region labelled \(\mu\). The stem already names both lens types and R losslessly, so the row is answerable from text; the drawing shows which curved surface faces which. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
Take the two lenses one at a time with the lens maker's formula, \(\dfrac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left[\dfrac{1}{R_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{R_{2}}\right]\), and then add their powers.
PLANO-CONVEX lens: one face is flat, so its radius is infinite and contributes nothing; the other has radius R.
\(\dfrac{1}{f_{1}} = (\mu - 1)\left[\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{\infty}\right] = \dfrac{\mu - 1}{R}\)
EQUI-CONCAVE lens: both faces are curved with radius R, and both curve the other way, so under the sign convention \(R_{1} = -R\) and \(R_{2} = +R\).
\(\dfrac{1}{f_{2}} = (\mu - 1)\left[-\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{R}\right] = -\dfrac{2(\mu - 1)}{R}\)
Thin lenses in contact add their powers:
\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{f_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{f_{2}} = \dfrac{\mu - 1}{R} - \dfrac{2(\mu - 1)}{R} = -\dfrac{\mu - 1}{R}\)
\(f = -\dfrac{R}{\mu - 1}\)
The combination is therefore DIVERGING: the concave lens has two curved surfaces working against the convex lens's one, so it wins.

rows.stem: The phase difference between the two superimposing waves that give rise to a bright spot in a Young's double-slit experiment is (n is an integer) :
rows.solution:
A bright fringe is constructive interference, which needs the two waves to arrive crest on crest.
The path difference for a maximum is a whole number of wavelengths, \(\Delta x = n\lambda\), and phase difference and path difference are related by
\(\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x\)
Substituting \(\Delta x = n\lambda\):
\(\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times n\lambda = 2n\pi\)
The phase difference is \(2n\pi\), that is a whole number of complete cycles. The option \(2n\pi + \pi\) is the condition for a DARK fringe, the waves arriving exactly out of step, and the two intermediate values give partial brightness rather than a maximum.

rows.stem: A telescope has an objective lens of focal length 144 cm and an eyepiece of focal length \(6{\cdot}0\) cm. The magnifying power and the length of telescope tube will be respectively :
rows.solution:
For a telescope in normal adjustment the final image is at infinity, and both quantities asked for follow from that.
MAGNIFYING POWER is the ratio of the two focal lengths:
\(m = \dfrac{f_{0}}{f_{e}} = \dfrac{144}{6{\cdot}0} = 24\)
LENGTH OF THE TUBE is their sum, since the objective's focal plane and the eyepiece's focal plane must coincide:
\(L = f_{0} + f_{e} = 144 + 6{\cdot}0 = 150\ \mathrm{cm}\)
The magnifying power and tube length are 24 and 150 cm. The distractor pairing 42 with 138 cm comes from dividing and subtracting the wrong way round: the tube must be LONGER than the objective's focal length, never shorter.

rows.stem: In which of the following, total internal reflection does **not** occur ?
rows.solution:
Total internal reflection needs light to strike a boundary from the DENSER side at more than the critical angle, and three of the four examples are exactly that.
A diamond's brilliance comes from its very high refractive index, which makes the critical angle small (about \(24^{\circ}\)), so light entering the stone is repeatedly totally internally reflected before it escapes. An optical fibre guides light down its core by total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary. A reflecting prism turns light through \(90^{\circ}\) or \(180^{\circ}\) by total internal reflection at its glass-air face, which is why it beats a silvered mirror.
The TWINKLING OF STARS is not a case of it. Starlight reaches us through air of continuously varying density and temperature, so it is REFRACTED through slightly different paths from moment to moment, and the apparent position and brightness flicker. There is no denser-to-rarer boundary and no critical angle involved.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem: Radiation of wavelength 200 nm is incident on a photosensitive surface of work function \(4{\cdot}2\) eV. The kinetic energy of fastest photoelectrons emitted from this surface will be close to :
rows.solution:
First find the energy each photon carries, using \(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}\) with the convenient form \(hc = 1240\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}\):
\(E = \dfrac{1240}{200} = 6{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{eV}\)
The FASTEST photoelectrons are those that needed only the minimum energy to escape, namely the work function. Einstein's photoelectric equation gives their kinetic energy:
\(K_{max} = E - \phi_{0} = 6{\cdot}2 - 4{\cdot}2 = 2{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{eV}\)
The kinetic energy of the fastest photoelectrons is about \(2{\cdot}0\) eV. Electrons emitted from below the surface lose some energy on the way out and arrive with less, which is why the equation gives a maximum rather than a single value.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem: A proton and an alpha particle have equal momentum. The ratio of their kinetic energies \((E_p / E_a)\) and de Broglie wavelengths associated with them \((\lambda_p / \lambda_a)\) respectively are :
rows.solution:
Both answers follow from writing each quantity in terms of the MOMENTUM, which the two particles share.
KINETIC ENERGY. For a non-relativistic particle \(K = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m}\), so with p the same for both, \(K \propto \dfrac{1}{m}\):
\(\dfrac{E_{p}}{E_{\alpha}} = \dfrac{m_{\alpha}}{m_{p}} = \dfrac{4}{1} = 4\)
An alpha particle is four times as massive as a proton, so at equal momentum it is the LIGHTER particle that carries the greater kinetic energy.
DE BROGLIE WAVELENGTH. \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}\) depends on the momentum alone, and nothing else. Equal momenta therefore mean equal wavelengths:
\(\dfrac{\lambda_{p}}{\lambda_{\alpha}} = 1\)
The two ratios are 4 and 1.

rows.stem: If \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) are the radii of atomic nuclei of mass numbers 64 and 27 respectively, then the value of \(\left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)\) is :
rows.solution:
Nuclear radii follow \(R = R_{0}A^{1/3}\), where A is the mass number. The cube root is the whole content of the question: nuclear volume is proportional to A, so the radius goes as the cube root of it, and nuclear matter has essentially the same density in every nucleus.
\(\dfrac{r_{1}}{r_{2}} = \left(\dfrac{A_{1}}{A_{2}}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\dfrac{64}{27}\right)^{1/3} = \dfrac{4}{3}\)
The ratio is \(\dfrac{4}{3}\). The numbers 64 and 27 were chosen as perfect cubes, so the arithmetic is exact; the option \(\dfrac{27}{64}\) is what a direct ratio of the mass numbers, inverted, would give.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: When the forward bias voltage in a semiconductor diode is changed from \(0{\cdot}8\) V to \(1{\cdot}0\) V, the forward current changes by \(2{\cdot}0\) mA. The forward bias resistance of the diode will be :
rows.solution:
The forward bias resistance of a diode is not \(\dfrac{V}{I}\) but the DYNAMIC resistance, the ratio of a small change in voltage to the change in current it produces, because the characteristic is strongly non-linear:
\(r_{d} = \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}\)
Here \(\Delta V = 1{\cdot}0 - 0{\cdot}8 = 0{\cdot}2\) V and \(\Delta I = 2{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{mA} = 2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3}\) A:
\(r_{d} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}2}{2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-3}} = 100\ \Omega\)
The forward bias resistance is \(100\ \Omega\). The forward characteristic rises very steeply beyond the knee voltage, so this value is small and falls further as the bias is raised, unlike the reverse resistance which runs into megohms.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: The process named 'minority carrier injection' in a p-n junction diode occurs during :
rows.solution:
Under FORWARD bias the external battery opposes the junction's built-in field, so the barrier height and the width of the depletion region both fall. Majority carriers can then cross: holes flow from the p-side into the n-side and electrons from the n-side into the p-side.
The point is what they become ON ARRIVAL. A hole that has crossed into the n-region is a MINORITY carrier there, and an electron that has crossed into the p-region is a minority carrier there. So forward bias raises the minority carrier concentration on each side well above its equilibrium value, and that is what is meant by minority carrier injection.
Under reverse bias the opposite happens: the barrier grows, majority carriers are held back, and the small current that flows is carried by minority carriers already present, which are swept across rather than injected.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : In a Wheatstone bridge circuit, if we interchange the position of the cell and the galvanometer, the balance condition \(\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S}\) remains unchanged.
Reason (R) : \(\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S} \Rightarrow \dfrac{Q}{S} = \dfrac{P}{R}\) so balance condition remains same.
rows.context: Questions number 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
The assertion is TRUE. A Wheatstone bridge balances when no current flows through the galvanometer, and the balance condition is symmetric in a way that survives swapping the cell and the galvanometer between the two diagonals. The bridge is balanced by the RATIOS of the four resistances, not by which diagonal carries the source.
The reason is also TRUE, and it is the correct explanation. Interchanging the cell and the galvanometer changes which pairs of arms are compared, so the condition is now written \(\dfrac{P}{R} = \dfrac{Q}{S}\). But cross-multiplying,
\(\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{R}{S} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad PS = QR \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \dfrac{P}{R} = \dfrac{Q}{S}\)
The two statements are the same equation rearranged, so a bridge balanced one way is balanced the other way, and the reason shows exactly why.
Both are true and the reason explains the assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The cylindrical soft iron core in a moving coil galvanometer only makes the magnetic field radial and does not affect the strength of the magnetic field.
Reason (R) : In a moving coil galvanometer, the plane of the coil is always perpendicular to the magnetic field.
rows.context: Questions number 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
Both statements are FALSE.
The ASSERTION is false because the soft iron core does TWO things, not one. Being a ferromagnetic material of high permeability, it concentrates the field lines through itself, which makes the field in the gap radial, and it also makes that field considerably STRONGER than the magnet alone would produce. Saying it "only" makes the field radial and leaves the strength untouched denies half of its purpose; a stronger field is what raises the galvanometer's current sensitivity.
The REASON is false because it states the geometry backwards. The point of the radial field is that the plane of the coil is always PARALLEL to the field lines, so the normal to the coil is perpendicular to the field and the angle between them stays at \(90^{\circ}\) whatever the deflection. That is what makes \(\sin\theta = 1\) always, and hence the deflection proportional to the current, giving a uniform scale.
Both the assertion and the reason are false.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Photoelectric Effect and its Experimental Study
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Photoelectric current depends upon the intensity of the incident radiation.
Reason (R) : Stopping potential is independent of the intensity of the incident radiation.
rows.context: Questions number 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
The assertion is TRUE. Raising the intensity of the incident light means delivering more photons per second, and each photon can liberate at most one electron, so the number of photoelectrons emitted per second, and hence the photoelectric current, rises in proportion to the intensity.
The reason is also TRUE. The stopping potential measures the MAXIMUM kinetic energy through \(eV_{0} = h\nu - \phi_{0}\), which contains the frequency and the work function but not the intensity. Brighter light of the same colour sends more photons, not more energetic ones, so the stopping potential does not shift.
But the reason is NOT the explanation of the assertion. The two statements are the two independent halves of the photoelectric result: intensity controls the NUMBER of electrons, frequency controls their ENERGY. A fact about what the stopping potential does not depend on cannot explain what the current does depend on.
Both are true and the reason is not the correct explanation.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Nuclear forces are always attractive.
Reason (R) : The nuclear force between protons and neutrons in a nucleus is a weak force.
rows.context: Questions number 13 to 16 are Assertion (A) and Reason (R) type questions. Two statements are given — one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are false.

rows.solution:
Both statements are FALSE.
The ASSERTION is false because the nuclear force reverses character at very short range. Between about \(0{\cdot}8\) fm and a few fm it is strongly attractive, which is what binds the nucleus, but below roughly \(0{\cdot}5\) fm it becomes strongly REPULSIVE. That short-range repulsion is essential: without it nucleons would collapse into one another and nuclei would have no fixed size.
The REASON is false because it names the wrong interaction. The force binding protons and neutrons is the STRONG nuclear force, the most powerful of the four fundamental interactions, some hundred times stronger than the electrostatic repulsion it has to overcome between protons. The WEAK nuclear force is a different interaction altogether, responsible for beta decay, not for binding.
Both the assertion and the reason are false.

rows.stem: In the given figure, a steady current I flows through the circuit when points A and C are connected by a wire of negligible resistance. Find the potential difference between points B and C.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - a single series branch drawn between terminals A and C with the junction B marked between them. It carries two cells with their internal resistances, labelled \(E_1 = 6\) V with \(1\ \Omega\) on the A-B side and \(E_2 = 4\) V with \(3\ \Omega\) on the B-C side; arrowheads on the branch mark the sense of the current I, and the cell symbols carry the polarity. Every numeric value and both directed quantities (current sense, cell polarity) exist only in the drawing, so the current sense and polarity are deliberately NOT stated here. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
With A and C joined by a resistanceless wire the two cells sit in a single closed loop, and they OPPOSE each other: the 6 V cell drives the current and the 4 V cell is driven backwards, so the net emf is the difference.
\(\varepsilon_{net} = \varepsilon_{1} - \varepsilon_{2} = 6 - 4 = 2\ \mathrm{V}\)
The two internal resistances are in series:
\(R_{net} = r_{1} + r_{2} = 1 + 3 = 4\ \Omega\)
\(I = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{net}}{R_{net}} = \dfrac{2}{4} = 0{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{A}\)
Now take the branch from B to C, which contains the 4 V cell and its \(3\ \Omega\) internal resistance. The current is being forced BACKWARDS through this cell, so it is being charged, and the potential rises across it in the direction of travel:
\(V_{B} - V_{C} = -\varepsilon_{2} - Ir_{2} = -4 - (0{\cdot}5 \times 3) = -5{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{V}\)
The potential difference between B and C is \(-5{\cdot}5\) V, so C is the higher of the two by \(5{\cdot}5\) V.
The sign is worth a check against the other branch: since the wire makes \(V_{A} = V_{C}\), the same reasoning along A to B must give \(+5{\cdot}5\) V, and indeed the 6 V cell is DISCHARGING, so its terminal voltage is \(6 - (0{\cdot}5 \times 1) = 5{\cdot}5\) V. The two agree.

rows.stem:
A battery of emf 21 V and internal resistance \(3\ \Omega\) is connected to a resistor. If the current in the circuit is 3 A, find :
(i) the resistance of the resistor.
(ii) the terminal voltage of the battery.
rows.solution:
(i) The emf is shared between the external resistor and the internal resistance of the battery:
\(\varepsilon = I(R + r) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad IR = \varepsilon - Ir\)
\(R = \dfrac{\varepsilon - Ir}{I} = \dfrac{21 - (3 \times 3)}{3} = \dfrac{12}{3} = 4\ \Omega\)
The resistance of the resistor is \(4\ \Omega\).
(ii) The terminal voltage is the potential difference actually available across the external resistor:
\(V = IR = 3 \times 4 = 12\ \mathrm{V}\)
The terminal voltage is 12 V.
It can be checked the other way: \(V = \varepsilon - Ir = 21 - 9 = 12\) V. The 9 V lost inside the battery is a large fraction of the emf here, because the internal resistance is comparable to the external one.

rows.stem: Explain why diffraction of sound is more common in daily experience than that of light.
rows.solution:
Diffraction becomes noticeable only when the obstacle or aperture is COMPARABLE IN SIZE to the wavelength. If the obstacle is very much larger, the wave casts a sharp shadow and travels in straight lines to a good approximation.
The wavelengths decide the outcome, and they differ by a factor of about a million. Audible sound has wavelengths from a few centimetres up to several metres, which is precisely the range of the doors, walls, furniture and people around us. Sound therefore bends around them readily, which is why a person speaking in the next room can be heard through an open doorway without being seen.
Visible light has wavelengths of only a few hundred nanometres, thousands of times smaller than any everyday obstacle. Ordinary objects are enormous on the scale of a light wave, so light appears to travel in straight lines and casts sharp shadows. Its diffraction has to be sought out deliberately, with a narrow slit or a fine grating of the right size.
So the difference is not in the nature of the two waves but in the scale of the obstacles they meet.

rows.stem: Explain the terms mass defect and binding energy. How are they related ?
rows.solution:
MASS DEFECT. The mass of any nucleus is found to be LESS than the sum of the masses of the free protons and neutrons that compose it. That difference is the mass defect:
\(\Delta M = \left[Zm_{p} + (A - Z)m_{n}\right] - M\)
where Z is the atomic number, A the mass number and M the actual mass of the nucleus.
BINDING ENERGY. When free nucleons are assembled into a nucleus, energy is RELEASED; equivalently, that much energy must be supplied to pull the nucleus apart into its separate nucleons again. That energy is the binding energy, and it is what holds the nucleus together.
THE RELATION between them is Einstein's mass-energy equivalence. The missing mass has not disappeared; it has been carried away as the released energy:
\(E_{b} = \Delta M c^{2} = \left[Zm_{p} + (A - Z)m_{n} - M\right]c^{2}\)
With masses in atomic mass units the conversion \(1\ \mathrm{u} = 931\ \mathrm{MeV}\) makes the arithmetic quick. A large mass defect means a tightly bound nucleus, and it is the binding energy PER NUCLEON, rather than the total, that decides which nuclei release energy on fission or fusion.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.stem: A particle of mass M at rest splits up into two particles of masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) having non-zero velocities. Calculate the ratio of the de Broglie wavelengths associated with the two particles.
rows.solution:
The parent particle is at rest, so the total momentum before the split is zero, and momentum is conserved:
\(m_{1}v_{1} - m_{2}v_{2} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad m_{1}v_{1} = m_{2}v_{2}\)
The two fragments therefore fly apart with momenta of EQUAL MAGNITUDE and opposite direction.
The de Broglie wavelength depends on the momentum alone:
\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{mv}\)
so
\(\dfrac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{2}} = \dfrac{h/m_{1}v_{1}}{h/m_{2}v_{2}} = \dfrac{m_{2}v_{2}}{m_{1}v_{1}} = 1\)
The ratio is \(\lambda_{1} : \lambda_{2} = 1 : 1\). The two wavelengths are equal WHATEVER the two masses turn out to be, because the masses never appear separately; only the product mv does, and conservation of momentum has already made the two products equal. The lighter fragment moves faster in exactly the proportion needed to compensate.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.stem: How are charge carriers created in an intrinsic semiconductor ? Explain.
rows.solution:
An intrinsic semiconductor is a pure crystal, such as silicon or germanium, in which every atom is bound to four neighbours by covalent bonds.
At absolute zero, and at very low temperatures, all these bonds are INTACT. Every valence electron is locked into a bond, none is free to move through the crystal, and the material behaves as an insulator.
As the temperature rises, thermal energy becomes available to the lattice. Some bonds absorb enough of it to break, and the electron that was shared in such a bond is set free to wander through the crystal. That free electron is one charge carrier.
The vacancy it leaves behind in the broken bond is the second. A neighbouring bound electron can move into this vacancy, which moves the vacancy in the opposite direction, so it behaves as a mobile particle carrying an effective POSITIVE charge. It is called a HOLE.
So the carriers are always created in PAIRS, one electron and one hole per broken bond, which is why an intrinsic semiconductor has \(n_{e} = n_{h} = n_{i}\). Their number, and hence the conductivity, rises rapidly with temperature, which is the opposite of what happens in a metal.

rows.stem:
(a) Establish the relation between drift velocity of electrons \((v_d)\) and electric current (I) in a conductor.
(b) How is \(v_d\) affected when the length of the conductor is doubled, keeping the voltage applied across the conductor constant ?
rows.solution:
(a) Consider a conductor of cross-sectional area A carrying n free electrons per unit volume, each of charge e, drifting with speed \(v_{d}\).
In a time \(\Delta t\) every electron moves a distance \(v_{d}\Delta t\), so all the electrons within a cylinder of length \(v_{d}\Delta t\) and cross-section A cross the far face. The number of such electrons is \(nAv_{d}\Delta t\), and the charge they carry is
\(Q = neAv_{d}\Delta t\)
The current is the charge crossing per unit time:
\(I = \dfrac{Q}{\Delta t} = neAv_{d}\)
This is the required relation. The drift speed itself is tiny, of the order of a millimetre per second, yet the current appears instantly when the circuit is closed, because the electric field that sets ALL the electrons drifting is established through the conductor at nearly the speed of light.
(b) The drift velocity is produced by the field inside the conductor, \(E = \dfrac{V}{l}\):
\(v_{d} = \dfrac{eE\tau}{m} = \dfrac{eV\tau}{ml}\)
With the applied voltage V held constant, \(v_{d} \propto \dfrac{1}{l}\). Doubling the length HALVES the drift velocity, because the same potential difference is now spread over twice the distance, so the field driving the electrons is only half as strong.

rows.subtopic: Torque on a Current Loop and Magnetic Dipole
rows.stem: A circular coil of 30 turns and radius \(8{\cdot}0\) cm carrying a current of 6 A is suspended vertically in a uniform horizontal magnetic field of \(1{\cdot}0\) T. The field lines make an angle of \(30^\circ\) with the plane of the coil. Calculate the magnitude of the external torque that must be applied to prevent the coil from turning. What would happen if the circular coil is replaced by a planar coil of irregular shape that encloses the same area, keeping other parameters unchanged ?
rows.solution:
The torque on a current-carrying coil in a uniform field is
\(\tau = NIBA\sin\theta\)
where \(\theta\) is the angle between the magnetic moment of the coil, which points along its NORMAL, and the field.
The angle is where this question is won or lost. The field lines make \(30^{\circ}\) with the PLANE of the coil, so with the normal they make \(90^{\circ} - 30^{\circ} = 60^{\circ}\). Hence \(\theta = 60^{\circ}\).
The area is \(A = \pi r^{2} = 3{\cdot}14 \times (8{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-2})^{2} = 3{\cdot}14 \times 64 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\). Substituting:
\(\tau = 30 \times 6 \times 1{\cdot}0 \times 3{\cdot}14 \times 64 \times 10^{-4} \times \sin 60^{\circ}\)
\(\tau = 3{\cdot}13\ \mathrm{N\,m}\)
Since the coil is to be held still, the external torque must balance this exactly, so its magnitude is \(3{\cdot}13\) N m.
IF THE COIL WERE REPLACED by a planar coil of irregular shape enclosing the same area, the torque would REMAIN THE SAME. The expression contains only the AREA enclosed, never the shape or the perimeter: the magnetic moment of any planar loop is \(NIA\) whatever its outline, so two flat coils of equal area and equal current are indistinguishable to the field.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: An alpha particle (mass \(6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-27}\) kg and charge \(3{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-19}\) C) having \(8{\cdot}0\) MeV energy, enters a region of a uniform magnetic field of \(0{\cdot}5\) T. If the field is directed perpendicular to the velocity of the particle, find the radius of the circular path described by the particle. Mention the condition under which the particle in this region (i) describes a helical path, and (ii) goes straight undeviated.
rows.solution:
The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force, and the radius follows from the momentum:
\(qvB = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}\)
using \(K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\), so that \(mv = \sqrt{2mK}\).
The energy is \(K = 8{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{MeV} = 8 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^{6} = 1{\cdot}28 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{J}\). Substituting:
\(r = \dfrac{\sqrt{2 \times 1{\cdot}28 \times 10^{-12} \times 6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-27}}}{3{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-19} \times 0{\cdot}5} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}28 \times 10^{-19}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}}\)
\(r = 0{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{m} = 80\ \mathrm{cm}\)
(i) HELICAL PATH. The particle must enter at an angle \(\theta\) with the field where \(0^{\circ} < \theta < 90^{\circ}\). The velocity component perpendicular to the field is bent into a circle while the component along the field is untouched by the magnetic force, and the two together wind the path into a helix.
(ii) STRAIGHT AND UNDEVIATED. The particle must move PARALLEL or ANTIPARALLEL to the field. Then \(\vec{v} \times \vec{B} = 0\), the magnetic force vanishes entirely, and the particle sails through the region as if the field were not there.

rows.subtopic: AC Voltage Applied to an Inductor and a Capacitor
rows.stem:
(a) Discuss the behaviour of an inductor connected to (i) a dc source, and (ii) a high frequency ac source.
(b) What is the phase relation between current and voltage in an ideal inductor connected to an ac source ? Draw a phasor diagram for the circuit.
rows.solution:
(a) The inductor's opposition to current is its reactance, \(X_{L} = \omega L = 2\pi\nu L\), and the whole of its behaviour follows from the frequency appearing in that formula.
(i) ON A dc SOURCE the steady-state frequency is zero, so \(X_{L} = 0\). At the instant the circuit is switched on the inductor does oppose the rising current, by inducing a back emf, but once the current has become steady there is no further change of flux, no back emf, and the inductor offers only the resistance of its own winding. It then behaves essentially as a plain CONDUCTOR.
(ii) ON A HIGH FREQUENCY ac SOURCE the current is reversing rapidly, so the flux through the coil changes rapidly and a large back emf is induced continuously. The reactance \(X_{L} = 2\pi\nu L\) is large, and the inductor BLOCKS the current. This is why an inductor is used as a choke: it passes dc and low frequencies freely while obstructing high ones.
(b) In an ideal inductor the CURRENT LAGS the voltage by a quarter of a cycle, that is by \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) radian. The reason is that the induced emf depends on the RATE OF CHANGE of current rather than on the current itself, so the current is still climbing when the voltage has already peaked and fallen back to zero.
PHASOR DIAGRAM: draw the current phasor I and the voltage phasor V from a common origin, both rotating anticlockwise with angular velocity \(\omega\), with V drawn a quarter turn AHEAD of I, so that the angle between them is \(90^{\circ}\). Because the phase difference is exactly \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), the average power consumed over a full cycle is zero: an ideal inductor stores energy in its magnetic field during one quarter cycle and returns all of it during the next.

rows.stem:
(a) Depict the variation of electric field \((\vec{E})\) and magnetic field \((\vec{B})\) with respect to the direction of propagation of an electromagnetic wave. Write their two important characteristics.
(b) Show that \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_0 \mu_0}}\) gives the velocity of an electromagnetic wave in free space.
rows.solution:
(a) VARIATION OF THE FIELDS. Draw the direction of propagation along one axis, say the z-axis. The electric field \(\vec{E}\) oscillates sinusoidally in the x-z plane, along the x-direction; the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) oscillates sinusoidally in the y-z plane, along the y-direction. The two oscillations are IN PHASE, reaching their maxima and their zeros at the same points, and each is perpendicular both to the other and to the direction of travel:
\(E_{x} = E_{0}\sin(kz - \omega t), \qquad B_{y} = B_{0}\sin(kz - \omega t)\)
Two important characteristics:
- The wave is TRANSVERSE: \(\vec{E}\), \(\vec{B}\) and the direction of propagation are mutually perpendicular, with \(\vec{E} \times \vec{B}\) pointing along the direction of travel.
- It needs NO MATERIAL MEDIUM and travels through vacuum at \(3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\); the amplitudes are locked together by \(\dfrac{E_{0}}{B_{0}} = c\).
(b) Maxwell's equations give the speed of an electromagnetic wave in free space as \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}}}\). Substituting the measured constants \(\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{0} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi \times 9 \times 10^{9}}\ \mathrm{C^{2}N^{-1}m^{-2}}\):
\(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{1}{4\pi \times 9 \times 10^{9}}}} = \sqrt{9 \times 10^{16}} = 3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
which is precisely the measured speed of light. The two constants were obtained from purely electrical and magnetic experiments with no reference to light at all, so their combination reproducing c is the evidence that light IS an electromagnetic wave.

rows.stem: A ray of light is travelling through a rectangular glass slab (refractive index \(\dfrac{3}{2}\)) and is incident on the horizontal glass-air surface at the critical angle for the two media. The slab is then brought in contact with water (refractive index \(\dfrac{4}{3}\)) such that a thin horizontal layer of water is formed on the surface of the slab. Find the angle at which the ray will emerge into air from the water-air surface.
rows.solution:
Work through the two boundaries in turn, and the answer falls out of Snell's law applied twice.
AT THE GLASS-AIR SURFACE, before the water is added, the ray arrives at the critical angle, so
\(\sin i_{c} = \dfrac{1}{n_{g}} = \dfrac{1}{3/2} = \dfrac{2}{3}\)
AT THE GLASS-WATER SURFACE, once the layer is added, the same ray strikes at that same angle \(i_{c}\), and refracts into the water at an angle r:
\(n_{g}\sin i_{c} = n_{w}\sin r\)
\(\dfrac{3}{2} \times \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}\sin r \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sin r = \dfrac{3}{4}\)
AT THE WATER-AIR SURFACE the ray meets the top boundary at this same angle r, and emerges into air at an angle e:
\(n_{w}\sin r = 1 \times \sin e\)
\(\dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{3}{4} = \sin e \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sin e = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e = 90^{\circ}\)
The ray emerges at \(90^{\circ}\) to the normal, that is GRAZING along the water-air surface.
The result is not a coincidence. In a stack of parallel layers the quantity \(n\sin\theta\) is the same in every layer, so it is fixed by the glass alone; the water drops out entirely. A ray that was exactly at the critical angle for glass-air is therefore exactly at the critical angle for water-air as well, whatever the intermediate medium happens to be.

rows.stem: Differentiate between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion. Give one example for each with nuclear reaction.
rows.solution:
THE DIFFERENCE. Nuclear FISSION is the splitting of a single heavy nucleus into two or more lighter fragments of intermediate mass, usually triggered by the absorption of a neutron. Nuclear FUSION is the joining of two light nuclei into a single heavier one.
Both release energy, and for the same underlying reason: the binding energy per nucleon peaks near mass number 56, so heavy nuclei gain by breaking up and light nuclei gain by combining. Both therefore move their products TOWARDS that peak from opposite sides.
They differ sharply in what it takes to start them. Fission needs only a slow neutron, which feels no electrostatic repulsion; fusion requires the two nuclei to be driven together against their mutual Coulomb repulsion, which needs temperatures of millions of kelvin, as found in the interior of the Sun.
EXAMPLE OF FISSION:
\(^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n} + ^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U} \rightarrow ^{144}_{56}\mathrm{Ba} + ^{89}_{36}\mathrm{Kr} + 3\,^{1}_{0}\mathrm{n}\)
The three neutrons released can each trigger a further fission, which is what makes a chain reaction possible.
EXAMPLE OF FUSION:
\(^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} + ^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} \rightarrow ^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + e^{+} + \nu + Q\)
This is the first step of the proton-proton cycle by which the Sun generates its energy.

rows.chapter: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
rows.subtopic: p-n Junction and the Semiconductor Diode
rows.stem: With the help of circuit diagrams, briefly explain the forward biasing and the reverse biasing of a p-n junction diode.
rows.solution:
FORWARD BIASING. Connect the p-side of the diode to the POSITIVE terminal of the battery and the n-side to the negative terminal, with a milliammeter in series to read the current and a voltmeter across the diode. The applied voltage opposes the junction's own built-in potential, so the barrier height is REDUCED and the depletion region narrows. Majority carriers can then cross in large numbers, holes from p to n and electrons from n to p, and a current of the order of MILLIAMPERES flows. Beyond the knee voltage, about \(0{\cdot}7\) V for silicon, the current rises very steeply for a small further increase of voltage, so the forward resistance is low.
REVERSE BIASING. Connect the p-side to the NEGATIVE terminal and the n-side to the positive terminal, now with a microammeter in series, because the current to be measured is far smaller. The applied voltage now acts in the SAME sense as the built-in potential, so the barrier is RAISED and the depletion region widens. Majority carriers are pushed away from the junction and cannot cross. Only the few minority carriers, thermally generated on the wrong side, are swept across, giving a tiny reverse saturation current of the order of MICROAMPERES which is almost independent of the applied voltage; it depends on temperature instead. The reverse resistance is therefore very high.
This sharp asymmetry between the two directions is precisely what makes a diode useful as a rectifier.

rows.stem: The total capacitance of the circuit is :
rows.context:
Capacitors are manufactured with certain standard capacitances and working voltages. However, these standard values may not be the ones that are actually needed in a particular application. Two or more capacitors can be grouped in series or in parallel to achieve desired capacitance and voltage. When connected in series, the total capacitance decreases while the voltage rating increases, whereas in parallel connections, the total capacitance increases and maintains the same voltage rating. A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its plates and stored energy is proportional to the square of the voltage and capacitance \(U = \dfrac{1}{2} CV^2\), where symbols have their usual meanings.
Two capacitors, one of \(3\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) and the other of \(6\ \mu\mathrm{F}\), are connected in series in the circuit as shown in the figure, for a long time.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - a circuit drawing. It shows a cell labelled 3 V, a resistor labelled \(5\ \Omega\), a resistor labelled \(10\ \Omega\), and the two capacitors labelled \(6\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) and \(3\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) in a branch whose ends are marked A and B with the point P between them. The cell voltage and both resistances appear NOWHERE in the passage, and the topology (which element is in series with which, and which branch carries the steady current) is exactly what every sub-part tests, so it is deliberately not described here. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
The two capacitors are joined end to end in the same branch, so the same charge sits on each: they are in SERIES, and series capacitances add as reciprocals.
\(\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{C_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{C_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{2 + 1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
\(C = 2\ \mu\mathrm{F}\)
The total capacitance is \(2\ \mu\mathrm{F}\). Note that it is SMALLER than either capacitor on its own, which is the defining behaviour of a series combination and is what the passage means by the total capacitance decreasing while the voltage rating increases. Adding the two values to get \(9\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) would be the parallel result.

rows.stem: The current in the \(10\ \Omega\) resistor is :
rows.context:
Capacitors are manufactured with certain standard capacitances and working voltages. However, these standard values may not be the ones that are actually needed in a particular application. Two or more capacitors can be grouped in series or in parallel to achieve desired capacitance and voltage. When connected in series, the total capacitance decreases while the voltage rating increases, whereas in parallel connections, the total capacitance increases and maintains the same voltage rating. A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its plates and stored energy is proportional to the square of the voltage and capacitance \(U = \dfrac{1}{2} CV^2\), where symbols have their usual meanings.
Two capacitors, one of \(3\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) and the other of \(6\ \mu\mathrm{F}\), are connected in series in the circuit as shown in the figure, for a long time.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the same circuit drawing as Q29 (i); the cell voltage and both resistances are stated only there. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
The phrase "for a long time" is the key: the circuit has reached its STEADY STATE. Once the capacitors are fully charged no further charge flows onto their plates, so the branch containing them carries NO current at all.
The current therefore has only one path available, through the \(5\ \Omega\) resistor and the \(10\ \Omega\) resistor, which are in series across the 3 V cell:
\(I = \dfrac{V}{R_{1} + R_{2}} = \dfrac{3}{5 + 10} = \dfrac{3}{15} = 0{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{A}\)
The current in the \(10\ \Omega\) resistor is \(0{\cdot}2\) A. A capacitor is an open circuit to steady current but is not "absent": it still holds a potential difference, as the next parts use.

rows.stem: The potential difference between point A and B is :
rows.context:
Capacitors are manufactured with certain standard capacitances and working voltages. However, these standard values may not be the ones that are actually needed in a particular application. Two or more capacitors can be grouped in series or in parallel to achieve desired capacitance and voltage. When connected in series, the total capacitance decreases while the voltage rating increases, whereas in parallel connections, the total capacitance increases and maintains the same voltage rating. A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its plates and stored energy is proportional to the square of the voltage and capacitance \(U = \dfrac{1}{2} CV^2\), where symbols have their usual meanings.
Two capacitors, one of \(3\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) and the other of \(6\ \mu\mathrm{F}\), are connected in series in the circuit as shown in the figure, for a long time.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the same circuit drawing as Q29 (i); the points A and B, the cell voltage and both resistances are marked only there. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
Points A and B are the two ends of the \(10\ \Omega\) resistor, and the capacitor branch is connected across the same two points.
Since the steady current through the \(10\ \Omega\) resistor is \(0{\cdot}2\) A, Ohm's law gives
\(V_{AB} = IR = 0{\cdot}2 \times 10 = 2\ \mathrm{V}\)
The potential difference between A and B is 2 V.
The remaining 1 V of the cell's 3 V is dropped across the \(5\ \Omega\) resistor, \(0{\cdot}2 \times 5 = 1\) V, and the two account for the whole emf. This 2 V is also the voltage across the series capacitor combination, since it hangs between the same pair of points.

rows.stem: The value of charge on the plates of the \(6\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) capacitor is :
rows.context:
Capacitors are manufactured with certain standard capacitances and working voltages. However, these standard values may not be the ones that are actually needed in a particular application. Two or more capacitors can be grouped in series or in parallel to achieve desired capacitance and voltage. When connected in series, the total capacitance decreases while the voltage rating increases, whereas in parallel connections, the total capacitance increases and maintains the same voltage rating. A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its plates and stored energy is proportional to the square of the voltage and capacitance \(U = \dfrac{1}{2} CV^2\), where symbols have their usual meanings.
Two capacitors, one of \(3\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) and the other of \(6\ \mu\mathrm{F}\), are connected in series in the circuit as shown in the figure, for a long time.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the same circuit drawing as Q29 (i); the cell voltage and both resistances are stated only there. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
In a SERIES combination the same charge resides on every capacitor, and that charge is fixed by the combined capacitance and the voltage across the whole branch.
The branch is connected between A and B, across which the potential difference is 2 V, and the combined capacitance is \(2\ \mu\mathrm{F}\):
\(Q = C V_{AB} = 2\ \mu\mathrm{F} \times 2\ \mathrm{V} = 4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)
The charge on the plates of the \(6\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) capacitor is \(4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\).
The \(3\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) capacitor carries exactly the same \(4\ \mu\mathrm{C}\); what differs between them is the VOLTAGE each takes, \(\dfrac{4}{6}\) V and \(\dfrac{4}{3}\) V, which sum to the 2 V across the branch. Using the larger capacitance with the full 2 V, giving \(12\ \mu\mathrm{C}\), is the trap here.

rows.stem: The wire between two capacitors is cut at point P. The current in the circuit will :
rows.context:
Capacitors are manufactured with certain standard capacitances and working voltages. However, these standard values may not be the ones that are actually needed in a particular application. Two or more capacitors can be grouped in series or in parallel to achieve desired capacitance and voltage. When connected in series, the total capacitance decreases while the voltage rating increases, whereas in parallel connections, the total capacitance increases and maintains the same voltage rating. A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its plates and stored energy is proportional to the square of the voltage and capacitance \(U = \dfrac{1}{2} CV^2\), where symbols have their usual meanings.
Two capacitors, one of \(3\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) and the other of \(6\ \mu\mathrm{F}\), are connected in series in the circuit as shown in the figure, for a long time.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the same circuit drawing as Q29 (i). The point P exists ONLY in the drawing, so this stem is unanswerable without it. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
Cutting the wire at P breaks the branch containing the two capacitors. That branch, however, was carrying NO current in the steady state, since a fully charged capacitor passes none.
Removing a path that carries no current changes nothing about the rest of the circuit. The cell still drives its current through the \(5\ \Omega\) and \(10\ \Omega\) resistors in series, and
\(I = \dfrac{3}{15} = 0{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{A}\)
as before. The current in the circuit will REMAIN THE SAME.
What the cut does change is the capacitors themselves: each keeps the charge it already held, now with nowhere to go, so they stay charged indefinitely instead of being able to discharge back through the circuit.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: The ratio of their kinetic energies \(\left(\dfrac{K_1}{K_2}\right)\) is :
rows.context: A charged particle +q in an electric field \(\vec{E}\) experiences a force in the direction of the electric field. As a result, its kinetic energy changes. Similarly, the charged particle also experiences a force when it moves in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\). But this magnetic force is perpendicular to both velocity \(\vec{v}\) of the charged particle and the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\), so it cannot change the kinetic energy of the charged particle. Consider two charged particles 1 and 2 of masses m and \(\dfrac{m}{2}\) having charges \(-q\) and \(+2q\) respectively. They are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference V and acquire kinetic energy \(K_1\) and \(K_2\). Then they enter in a region of uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) perpendicular to their velocities.
rows.solution:
Both particles start from rest and are accelerated through the same potential difference V, so the work done on each is the product of its own charge and that potential difference:
\(K = qV\)
For particle 1, of charge \(-q\), the magnitude of the work done is \(K_{1} = qV\). For particle 2, of charge \(+2q\), it is \(K_{2} = 2qV\).
\(\dfrac{K_{1}}{K_{2}} = \dfrac{qV}{2qV} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
The ratio is \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). The MASSES do not enter at all: a heavier particle emerges more slowly from the same accelerating voltage, but with the same kinetic energy as a lighter one of equal charge.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: The ratio of the radii of the circular paths described by them \(\left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)\) is :
rows.context: A charged particle +q in an electric field \(\vec{E}\) experiences a force in the direction of the electric field. As a result, its kinetic energy changes. Similarly, the charged particle also experiences a force when it moves in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\). But this magnetic force is perpendicular to both velocity \(\vec{v}\) of the charged particle and the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\), so it cannot change the kinetic energy of the charged particle. Consider two charged particles 1 and 2 of masses m and \(\dfrac{m}{2}\) having charges \(-q\) and \(+2q\) respectively. They are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference V and acquire kinetic energy \(K_1\) and \(K_2\). Then they enter in a region of uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) perpendicular to their velocities.
rows.solution:
The radius of the circular path is set by the momentum:
\(r = \dfrac{mv}{qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}\)
For particle 1, of mass m, charge magnitude q and kinetic energy \(K_{1} = qV\):
\(r_{1} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2m \cdot qV}}{qB}\)
For particle 2, of mass \(\dfrac{m}{2}\), charge \(2q\) and kinetic energy \(K_{2} = 2qV\):
\(r_{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2 \cdot \dfrac{m}{2} \cdot 2qV}}{2qB} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2mqV}}{2qB}\)
The two numerators are identical, \(\sqrt{2mqV}\), so the ratio comes entirely from the charges in the denominators:
\(\dfrac{r_{1}}{r_{2}} = 2\)
Particle 2, though it carries twice the kinetic energy, travels on a circle of half the radius, because its charge is twice as large and its mass half as great: both changes tighten the turn.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: Suppose particles 1 and 2 enter the magnetic field \(\vec{B} = B_0 \hat{k}\) with velocities \(\vec{v_1} = v_1 \hat{i}\) and \(\vec{v_2} = v_2 \hat{i}\). Then :
rows.context: A charged particle +q in an electric field \(\vec{E}\) experiences a force in the direction of the electric field. As a result, its kinetic energy changes. Similarly, the charged particle also experiences a force when it moves in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\). But this magnetic force is perpendicular to both velocity \(\vec{v}\) of the charged particle and the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\), so it cannot change the kinetic energy of the charged particle. Consider two charged particles 1 and 2 of masses m and \(\dfrac{m}{2}\) having charges \(-q\) and \(+2q\) respectively. They are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference V and acquire kinetic energy \(K_1\) and \(K_2\). Then they enter in a region of uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) perpendicular to their velocities.

options.label: C
options.text: particle 1 revolves clockwise while particle 2 revolves anticlockwise

options.label: D
options.text: particle 1 revolves anticlockwise while particle 2 revolves clockwise

rows.solution:
The sense of rotation is decided by the direction of the magnetic force, \(\vec{F} = q\vec{v} \times \vec{B}\), and the SIGN of the charge reverses it.
With \(\vec{B} = B_{0}\hat{k}\) and \(\vec{v} = v\hat{i}\), the cross product is
\(\hat{i} \times \hat{k} = -\hat{j}\)
PARTICLE 1 carries charge \(-q\), so
\(\vec{F}_{1} = (-q)(v_{1}B_{0})(-\hat{j}) = +qv_{1}B_{0}\,\hat{j}\)
The force is along \(+\hat{j}\), that is at right angles to the left of a particle moving along \(+\hat{i}\), so the particle turns towards the \(+y\) direction and revolves ANTICLOCKWISE in the xy-plane.
PARTICLE 2 carries charge \(+2q\), so
\(\vec{F}_{2} = (2q)(v_{2}B_{0})(-\hat{j}) = -2qv_{2}B_{0}\,\hat{j}\)
The force is along \(-\hat{j}\), so this particle turns the other way and revolves CLOCKWISE.
Particle 1 revolves anticlockwise while particle 2 revolves clockwise. The velocities being in the same direction is deliberate: the only thing separating the two answers is the sign of the charge.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: If period of revolution for particle 1 is 4 s, then for particle 2, the period will be :
rows.context: A charged particle +q in an electric field \(\vec{E}\) experiences a force in the direction of the electric field. As a result, its kinetic energy changes. Similarly, the charged particle also experiences a force when it moves in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\). But this magnetic force is perpendicular to both velocity \(\vec{v}\) of the charged particle and the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\), so it cannot change the kinetic energy of the charged particle. Consider two charged particles 1 and 2 of masses m and \(\dfrac{m}{2}\) having charges \(-q\) and \(+2q\) respectively. They are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference V and acquire kinetic energy \(K_1\) and \(K_2\). Then they enter in a region of uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) perpendicular to their velocities.
rows.solution:
The period of revolution in a magnetic field is
\(T = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}\)
and the striking feature of it is that the SPEED does not appear: a faster particle travels a larger circle in exactly the same time. So only the mass-to-charge ratio matters.
For particle 1: \(T_{1} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB} = 4\ \mathrm{s}\).
For particle 2, of mass \(\dfrac{m}{2}\) and charge \(2q\):
\(T_{2} = \dfrac{2\pi (m/2)}{(2q)B} = \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB} = \dfrac{T_{1}}{4} = \dfrac{4}{4} = 1\ \mathrm{s}\)
The period for particle 2 is 1 s. Halving the mass and doubling the charge each quarter the period between them, and this independence of speed is exactly the property a cyclotron relies on.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: If the value of momentum for particles 1 and 2 are \(p_1\) and \(p_2\), then :
rows.context: A charged particle +q in an electric field \(\vec{E}\) experiences a force in the direction of the electric field. As a result, its kinetic energy changes. Similarly, the charged particle also experiences a force when it moves in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\). But this magnetic force is perpendicular to both velocity \(\vec{v}\) of the charged particle and the magnetic field \(\vec{B}\), so it cannot change the kinetic energy of the charged particle. Consider two charged particles 1 and 2 of masses m and \(\dfrac{m}{2}\) having charges \(-q\) and \(+2q\) respectively. They are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference V and acquire kinetic energy \(K_1\) and \(K_2\). Then they enter in a region of uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) perpendicular to their velocities.
rows.solution:
Momentum and kinetic energy are related by \(p = \sqrt{2mK}\), and both particles' kinetic energies were fixed by the accelerating voltage.
For particle 1, of mass m and \(K_{1} = qV\):
\(p_{1} = \sqrt{2m \cdot qV} = \sqrt{2mqV}\)
For particle 2, of mass \(\dfrac{m}{2}\) and \(K_{2} = 2qV\):
\(p_{2} = \sqrt{2 \cdot \dfrac{m}{2} \cdot 2qV} = \sqrt{2mqV}\)
The two are EQUAL: \(p_{1} = p_{2}\).
Particle 2 has twice the kinetic energy but half the mass, and in \(\sqrt{2mK}\) those two factors cancel exactly. It is the same conclusion as the radius question seen from another angle, since \(r = \dfrac{p}{qB}\): equal momenta with unequal charges is precisely why the radii came out in the ratio 2 to 1.

rows.subtopic: Electrostatic Potential due to Charges and Dipoles
rows.stem:
(i) In the figure, OA and OB show the variation of electric potential V at a point due to two point charges \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) with \(\dfrac{1}{r}\) respectively. Here r represents the distance of the point from the two point charges.
(I) Identify the nature of the two charges \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\).
(II) What is the value of \(\left(\dfrac{Q_1}{Q_2}\right)\) ? Justify your answer.
(ii) Two point charges \(-2\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) and \(5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) are placed at \((-30\ \mathrm{cm},\, 0)\) and \((30\ \mathrm{cm},\, 0)\) respectively in an external electric field \(\vec{E} = \dfrac{A}{x^2}\hat{i}\), where \(A = 9 \times 10^5\ \mathrm{N m^2 C^{-1}}\). Find the electrostatic potential energy of this configuration.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - a graph with the vertical axis labelled V and the horizontal axis labelled \(\dfrac{1}{r}\), origin O, carrying two straight lines through the origin labelled A and B with their inclinations to the horizontal axis marked in degrees. WITHHELD deliberately: which line lies above the horizontal axis and which below (that is what part (I) asks) and the two angle values (that is what part (II) asks). Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
(i) The potential due to a point charge is \(V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{Q}{r}\), so a graph of V against \(\dfrac{1}{r}\) is a STRAIGHT LINE through the origin whose slope is \(\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\). The slope therefore carries both the size and the sign of the charge.
(I) Line OA rises above the axis, so its slope is positive and \(Q_{1}\) is a POSITIVE charge. Line OB falls below the axis, so its slope is negative and \(Q_{2}\) is a NEGATIVE charge.
(II) [CBSE marking scheme: it identifies \(Q_{2}\) as negative in part (I) and then evaluates the ratio as \(\dfrac{\tan 60^{\circ}}{\tan 30^{\circ}} = 3\), which silently drops that minus sign. The printed question asks for \(\left(\dfrac{Q_{1}}{Q_{2}}\right)\) in ordinary brackets, not for its modulus, so the signed value is required and the scheme's own part (I) contradicts its part (II). The magnitude, 3, is right.]
Since the slope is proportional to the charge, the ratio of the charges is the ratio of the slopes. OA makes \(60^{\circ}\) with the \(\dfrac{1}{r}\) axis, measured above it, and OB makes \(30^{\circ}\) below it:
\(\dfrac{Q_{1}}{Q_{2}} = \dfrac{\text{slope of OA}}{\text{slope of OB}} = \dfrac{\tan 60^{\circ}}{-\tan 30^{\circ}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{-1/\sqrt{3}} = -3\)
So \(\dfrac{Q_{1}}{Q_{2}} = -3\): the charges are opposite in sign and \(Q_{1}\) is three times the size of \(Q_{2}\).
(ii) The configuration sits in an EXTERNAL field, so the energy has three parts: each charge in the external field, plus the mutual energy of the pair.
The potential of the external field follows by integrating it:
\(V(x) = -\int E\,dx = -\int \dfrac{A}{x^{2}}dx = \dfrac{A}{x}\)
Hence
\(U = q_{1}V(x_{1}) + q_{2}V(x_{2}) + \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\dfrac{q_{1}q_{2}}{x_{12}}\)
With \(q_{1} = -2\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at 30 cm, \(q_{2} = 5\ \mu\mathrm{C}\) at 30 cm, a separation \(x_{12} = 60\) cm and \(A = 9 \times 10^{5}\):
\(U = \dfrac{-2 \times 10^{-6} \times 9 \times 10^{5}}{30 \times 10^{-2}} + \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-6} \times 9 \times 10^{5}}{30 \times 10^{-2}} - \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 5 \times 10^{-12}}{60 \times 10^{-2}}\)
\(U = (-6) + (15) - (0{\cdot}15) = 8{\cdot}85\ \mathrm{J}\)
The electrostatic potential energy of the configuration is \(8{\cdot}85\) J. The mutual term is negative because the charges are opposite, and it is by far the smallest of the three here.

rows.stem:
(i) Two infinitely long straight wires having linear charge densities \(-\lambda\) and \(3\lambda\) are held vertically parallel to each other, distance r apart in free space. Find the nature and magnitude of the force/length exerted by one wire on the other.
(ii) A small hollow conducting sphere of radius \(r_1\) is given a charge Q. It is surrounded by a concentric conducting spherical shell of inner radius \(r_2\) and outer radius \(r_3\), having charge \(-3q\).
If a point charge 2q were kept at the centre, find :
(I) the electric flux through a concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius x for (1) \(x < r_1\), and (2) \(r_1 < x < r_2\).
(II) electric field at a point distant x from the centre for (1) \(x > r_3\), and (2) \(r_1 < x < r_2\).
(III) surface charge density on the inner surface of (1) sphere, and (2) shell.
rows.solution:
(i) The field of one infinite line charge at perpendicular distance r is \(E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\), directed radially.
The second wire, of linear density \(3\lambda\), sits in this field, so a length l of it carries charge \(3\lambda l\) and experiences a force
\(\dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{(-\lambda)(3\lambda)}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}r} = -\dfrac{3\lambda^{2}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\)
The magnitude of the force per unit length is \(\dfrac{3\lambda^{2}}{2\pi\varepsilon_{0}r}\), and its NATURE IS ATTRACTIVE, since the two densities are of opposite sign. By Newton's third law the first wire feels an equal and opposite pull, so the same expression describes the force on either.
(ii) The arrangement, from the centre outwards: a point charge \(2q\) at the centre, a hollow conducting sphere of radius \(r_{1}\) carrying Q, and a conducting shell from \(r_{2}\) to \(r_{3}\) carrying \(-3q\).
(I) FLUX, which by Gauss's theorem depends only on the charge ENCLOSED.
(1) For \(x < r_{1}\) the Gaussian surface encloses the central point charge alone:
\(\phi = \dfrac{2q}{\varepsilon_{0}}\)
(2) For \(r_{1} < x < r_{2}\) it encloses the point charge and the whole sphere:
\(\phi = \dfrac{Q + 2q}{\varepsilon_{0}}\)
(II) ELECTRIC FIELD, from \(E \times 4\pi x^{2} = \dfrac{q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_{0}}\).
(1) For \(x > r_{3}\) everything is enclosed, \(2q + Q - 3q = Q - q\):
\(E = \dfrac{k(Q - q)}{x^{2}}\)
(2) For \(r_{1} < x < r_{2}\), in the gap between sphere and shell:
\(E = \dfrac{k(Q + 2q)}{x^{2}}\)
(III) SURFACE CHARGE DENSITY on the inner surfaces. The field inside the body of a conductor is zero, so any Gaussian surface drawn within the conducting material must enclose zero net charge. That fixes each induced inner charge.
(1) On the inner surface of the SPHERE, the induced charge must cancel the central \(2q\), so it is \(-2q\):
\(\sigma = \dfrac{-2q}{4\pi r_{1}^{2}}\)
(2) On the inner surface of the SHELL, the induced charge must cancel everything within it, that is \(2q + Q\):
\(\sigma = \dfrac{-(Q + 2q)}{4\pi r_{2}^{2}}\)

rows.stem:
(i) A light bulb and an open coil inductor are connected in series across an ac source of variable frequency. How will the glow of the bulb be affected when :
(I) an iron bar is inserted inside the coil, and
(II) the frequency of the source is decreased ?
Justify your answers. Assume that in each above case other factors remain unchanged.
(ii) An ac voltage \(V = 280 \sin (100\pi t)\) volt is connected across a series LCR circuit in which \(R = 400\ \Omega\), \(L = \dfrac{5}{\pi}\) H and \(C = \dfrac{50}{\pi}\ \mu\mathrm{F}\). Taking \(\sqrt{2} = 1{\cdot}4\), calculate :
(I) impedance of the circuit.
(II) rms value of current that flows in the circuit.
(III) power factor of the circuit.
rows.solution:
(i) The bulb and the coil are in series, so they carry the same current, and the brightness of the bulb follows that current. The current is set by the impedance \(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + X_{L}^{2}}\) with \(X_{L} = 2\pi\nu L\).
(I) INSERTING AN IRON BAR. The self-inductance of a coil is proportional to the permeability of its core, \(L' = \mu_{r}L\), and iron has a large relative permeability. So L increases sharply, \(X_{L} = \omega L\) increases, the impedance rises and the current falls. A larger share of the applied voltage now appears across the inductor, leaving less for the bulb, and the bulb GROWS DIMMER.
(II) DECREASING THE FREQUENCY. Now \(X_{L} = 2\pi\nu L\) falls, the impedance falls and the current rises. Less voltage is dropped across the coil and more appears across the bulb, so the bulb GROWS BRIGHTER. In the limit of dc the coil would offer only the resistance of its winding.
(ii) From \(V = 280\sin(100\pi t)\): \(V_{0} = 280\) V and \(\omega = 100\pi\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}\).
\(X_{L} = \omega L = 100\pi \times \dfrac{5}{\pi} = 500\ \Omega\)
\(X_{C} = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{100\pi \times \dfrac{50}{\pi} \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{10^{6}}{100 \times 50} = 200\ \Omega\)
(I) IMPEDANCE:
\(Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_{L} - X_{C})^{2}} = \sqrt{(400)^{2} + (300)^{2}} = 500\ \Omega\)
(II) RMS CURRENT:
\(I_{rms} = \dfrac{V_{rms}}{Z} = \dfrac{V_{0}}{\sqrt{2}\,Z} = \dfrac{280}{1{\cdot}4 \times 500} = 0{\cdot}4\ \mathrm{A}\)
(III) POWER FACTOR:
\(\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = \dfrac{400}{500} = 0{\cdot}8\)
The circuit is inductive, since \(X_{L} > X_{C}\), so the current lags the voltage; a power factor of \(0{\cdot}8\) means \(80\%\) of the apparent power is actually dissipated.

rows.stem:
(i) State Lenz's law and explain that it follows the law of conservation of energy.
(ii) Write the dimensional formula for self-inductance.
The current in a coil changes from \(8{\cdot}0\) A to \(2{\cdot}0\) A in \(0{\cdot}6\) s. If an average emf induced in the coil is 50 V, calculate the self-inductance of the coil.
rows.solution:
(i) LENZ'S LAW states that the polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which OPPOSES the change in magnetic flux that produced it.
IT FOLLOWS FROM CONSERVATION OF ENERGY. Consider the north pole of a magnet being pushed towards a coil. The flux through the coil increases, so by Lenz's law the induced current circulates in the sense that makes the near face of the coil a NORTH pole, which repels the approaching magnet. Work must therefore be done against that repulsion to keep the magnet moving, and exactly that work reappears as the electrical energy dissipated in the coil.
Now suppose the law were the other way round and the induced current ASSISTED the change. The near face would become a south pole and attract the magnet, which would accelerate it, increasing the rate of change of flux, increasing the induced current, and so on without limit. Both kinetic and electrical energy would be created from nothing, and a suitable arrangement would be a perpetual motion machine. Since that is impossible, the induced effect must oppose the change.
(ii) DIMENSIONAL FORMULA. From \(\varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}\), \(L = \dfrac{\varepsilon\,dt}{dI}\), so the dimensions are those of (voltage x time / current):
\(\left[\mathrm{M\,L^{2}\,T^{-2}\,A^{-2}}\right]\)
CALCULATION. The magnitude of the average induced emf is \(|\varepsilon| = L\left|\dfrac{dI}{dt}\right|\), so
\(L = \dfrac{-\varepsilon\,\Delta t}{\Delta I} = \dfrac{-(50) \times 0{\cdot}6}{2{\cdot}0 - 8{\cdot}0} = \dfrac{-30}{-6} = 5\ \mathrm{H}\)
The self-inductance of the coil is 5 H. The current FELL, so \(\Delta I\) is negative; the two minus signs cancel and leave a positive inductance, as they must.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem:
(i) A point object is kept in front of a convex spherical surface of radius of curvature R. Draw the ray diagram to show the formation of image and derive the relation between the object and image distance (u and v) in terms of refractive index n of the medium and R.
(ii) A convex lens of focal length of 20 cm is used to form the image of an object placed 30 cm away from the lens. Find the position and nature of the image formed.
rows.solution:
(i) RAY DIAGRAM. Draw a convex spherical refracting surface separating a rarer medium on the left from a denser medium of refractive index n on the right, with pole M, centre of curvature C and radius R. Place a point object O on the principal axis in the rarer medium. Take one ray from O along the axis, which passes straight through, and a second ray ON striking the surface at N a small distance from the axis, which bends TOWARDS the normal CN on entering the denser medium. The two refracted rays meet at I on the axis, the real image.
DERIVATION. Let the angles of incidence and refraction at N be i and r. For a ray close to the axis all the angles are small, so each angle may be replaced by its tangent, and each tangent by the perpendicular MN over the appropriate distance:
\(\tan\angle NOM = \dfrac{MN}{MO}, \qquad \tan\angle NCM = \dfrac{MN}{MC}, \qquad \tan\angle NIM = \dfrac{MN}{MI}\)
The angle of incidence is an exterior angle of triangle NOC, so
\(i = \angle NOM + \angle NCM = \dfrac{MN}{MO} + \dfrac{MN}{MC}\)
and the angle of refraction is an exterior angle of triangle NCI:
\(r = \angle NCM - \angle NIM = \dfrac{MN}{MC} - \dfrac{MN}{MI}\)
Snell's law for small angles reads \(1 \times i = n \times r\). Substituting both expressions and cancelling MN:
\(\dfrac{1}{MO} + \dfrac{1}{MC} = n\left[\dfrac{1}{MC} - \dfrac{1}{MI}\right]\)
\(\dfrac{1}{MO} + \dfrac{n}{MI} = \dfrac{n - 1}{MC}\)
Applying the Cartesian sign convention, \(MO = -u\), \(MI = +v\) and \(MC = +R\):
\(\dfrac{n}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{n - 1}{R}\)
(ii) Using the lens formula \(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u}\) with \(f = +20\) cm and \(u = -30\) cm:
\(\dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{30} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{3 - 2}{60} = \dfrac{1}{60}\)
\(v = 60\ \mathrm{cm}\)
The image is formed 60 cm from the lens, on the side OPPOSITE the object, and since v is positive it is REAL and INVERTED. The magnification is \(m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{60}{-30} = -2\), so it is also magnified twofold, as expected for an object lying between f and 2f.

rows.stem:
(i) Two thin converging lenses of focal length \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) are placed coaxially in contact. Derive expression for the focal length of the combination.
(ii) A beam of coherent light of wavelength 550 nm is incident normal to the plane of a pair of two slits \(S_1\) and \(S_2\) each of width \(1{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-6}\) m separated by \(1{\cdot}1\) mm. Dark and bright fringes are observed on a screen \(2{\cdot}2\) m away from the plane of the slits.
Calculate :
(I) fringe width.
(II) distance of the second dark fringe from the central maximum.
(III) what will happen when the entire apparatus is immersed in water.
rows.solution:
(i) Let the two thin lenses A and B, of focal lengths \(f_{1}\) and \(f_{2}\), be placed in contact, and let an object O lie at a distance u from them.
Lens A alone would form an image at \(v_{1}\):
\(\dfrac{1}{v_{1}} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f_{1}}\)
This image now acts as the OBJECT for lens B. Because the lenses are in contact, the separation between them is negligible, so the object distance for B is the same \(v_{1}\), and B forms the final image at v:
\(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{v_{1}} = \dfrac{1}{f_{2}}\)
Adding the two equations, \(v_{1}\) cancels:
\(\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{f_{2}}\)
Comparing this with the lens formula for a single equivalent lens of focal length f:
\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{f_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{f_{2}}\)
In terms of power this reads \(P = P_{1} + P_{2}\): thin lenses in contact simply ADD their powers, which is why a combination is specified by powers rather than focal lengths.
(ii) (I) FRINGE WIDTH:
\(\beta = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{550 \times 10^{-9} \times 2{\cdot}2}{1{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-3}} = 1{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 1{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{mm}\)
(II) The DARK fringes lie where the path difference is an odd number of half wavelengths:
\(x_{n} = \dfrac{(2n - 1)\lambda D}{2d}\)
For the SECOND dark fringe, \(n = 2\):
\(x = \dfrac{3\lambda D}{2d} = \dfrac{3}{2}\beta = \dfrac{3}{2} \times 1{\cdot}1 = 1{\cdot}65\ \mathrm{mm}\)
(III) IMMERSED IN WATER the wavelength shortens to \(\dfrac{\lambda}{n}\), since the frequency is fixed by the source and the speed falls. The fringe width shortens in the same proportion:
\(\beta' = \dfrac{\beta}{n} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}1}{4/3} = 0{\cdot}825\ \mathrm{mm}\)
So the FRINGE WIDTH DECREASES and the whole pattern is squeezed towards the centre. The positions of the slits and the screen are unchanged, so the central maximum stays where it was.
